Nature Communications is an open access, multidisciplinary journal dedicated to publishing high-quality research in all areas of the biological, health, physical, chemical and Earth sciences. Papers published by the journal aim to represent important advances of significance to specialists within each field.

We are committed to providing an efficient service for both authors and readers. Our team of independent editors make rapid and fair publication decisions. Prompt dissemination of accepted papers to a wide readership and beyond is achieved through a programme of continuous online publication.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Neonatal overfeeding accelerates age-related sarcopenia and metabolic disorders through lifelong gut mucosa and microbiota programming in mice
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78216-2

Here, the authors demonstrate that neonatal overfeeding in mice shortens lifespan and accelerates late-life muscle loss. This originates from persistent gut mucus defects and depleted Akkermansia muciniphila, revealing a targetable developmental origin for sarcopenia.
ns1:item.dc:title: Neonatal overfeeding accelerates age-related sarcopenia and metabolic disorders through lifelong gut mucosa and microbiota programming in mice

ns1:item.ns1:title: High potential contribution of intercropping to soybean and maize self-sufficiency in Europe
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78206-4

Domestic production of maize and soybeans in the EU currently falls short of demand. This study finds that adoption of maize-soybean intercropping could improve soybean self-sufficiency by 25−91% but also contribute to EU maize demand by 50−145%.
ns1:item.dc:title: High potential contribution of intercropping to soybean and maize self-sufficiency in Europe

ns1:item.ns1:title: Ultrathin high-performance circular polarizers based on MoOCl<sub>2</sub>/NbOCl<sub>2</sub> van der Waals heterostructures
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78564-z

Circularly polarized light can be used in several applications, but normally requires bulky optical components. Here, the authors report the realization of sub-micron-thick circular polarizers based on the natural phase modulation capability of NbOCl2 and polarization selectivity of MoOCl2 crystals, showing their integration into a LED chip.
ns1:item.dc:title: Ultrathin high-performance circular polarizers based on MoOCl<sub>2</sub>/NbOCl<sub>2</sub> van der Waals heterostructures

ns1:item.ns1:title: Embryonic origin of cancer in newborn twins
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78178-5

Identical twins with the same cancer can reveal how childhood tumours arise and spread before birth. Here, the authors use whole-genome sequencing of tumour, normal and placental tissues to show that a sarcoma that originated in one twin spread to the other in utero, and trace early embryonic lineages that contributed differently to the twins and placenta.
ns1:item.dc:title: Embryonic origin of cancer in newborn twins

ns1:item.ns1:title: Distinct T cell correlates of COVID-19 risk before and after a second booster in previously SARS-CoV-2 infected versus naïve COVAIL trial participants
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78444-6

Vaccines to SARS-CoV-2 clearly stimulate virus specific T cell and antibody responses but T cell-mediated protection is challenging to show. Here the authors use PBMC samples from an open-label clinical trial of different prototype and variant-specific COVID-19 vaccine boosters to examine the function and phenotype of T cell populations and how T cell response levels associate with risk of, and with protection against, symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
ns1:item.dc:title: Distinct T cell correlates of COVID-19 risk before and after a second booster in previously SARS-CoV-2 infected versus naïve COVAIL trial participants

ns1:item.ns1:title: A generative diffusion framework for physically consistent 3D turbulence
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78265-7

Three-dimensional turbulence contains complex multiscale fluctuations that challenge even state-of-the-art generative models. Here, the authors develop a generative diffusion framework that produces physically consistent 3D turbulence with accurate multiscale statistics.
ns1:item.dc:title: A generative diffusion framework for physically consistent 3D turbulence
